title: Easements, Boundaries, Nuisance & Neighbor Disputes
originality: All items original to LicensePath. Modeled on the DRE exam blueprint and style only; no actual exam items reproduced.

questions.stem: An easement created by a written deed or specific agreement is an example of:
options: Prescription
Express grant
Necessity
Implication
rationales: Prescription arises from use, not a writing.
Correct. Express grant is created by a written instrument.
Necessity arises from landlocked circumstances, not a writing alone.
Implication arises from circumstances at severance, not a writing.

questions.stem: An easement by implication typically requires that the use, at the time of severance, was:
options: Secret and occasional
Apparent, continuous, and reasonably necessary
Created only by court order
Paid for with property taxes
rationales: Secret, occasional use does not support implication.
Correct. Apparent, continuous, reasonably necessary use at severance supports an implied easement.
Court order is not required for implication.
Tax payment is unrelated to easement by implication.

questions.stem: An easement by necessity generally requires:
options: Mere convenience of access
Strict necessity, such as a landlocked parcel from a prior division of commonly owned land
A recorded survey only
Continuous use for the statutory period
rationales: Mere convenience is not enough; strict necessity is required.
Correct. Easement by necessity requires strict necessity arising from a division of previously commonly owned land.
A recorded survey alone does not create this easement.
Statutory-period continuous use describes prescription, not necessity.

questions.stem: A prescriptive easement differs from adverse possession in ownership terms because a prescriptive easement:
options: Conveys full ownership of the land
Conveys only a right to use, not ownership
Requires payment of property taxes just like adverse possession
Cannot ever be established in California
rationales: Full ownership describes adverse possession, not a prescriptive easement.
Correct. A prescriptive easement grants only a right to use, not title.
Unlike adverse possession, prescriptive easements do not require tax payment.
Prescriptive easements can be established in California under the right facts.

questions.stem: A key distinction between a prescriptive easement and adverse possession is that:
options: Adverse possession does not require tax payment but prescription does
Prescription does not require tax payment on the servient land, while adverse possession does
Both require identical tax payment obligations
Neither requires open and notorious use
rationales: This reverses the actual rule.
Correct. Prescriptive easements do not require tax payment; adverse possession does.
Their tax requirements differ, not match.
Both generally require open and notorious use as an element.

options: Benefits a specific person, not land
Benefits a specific parcel and runs automatically with the land
Cannot be created by deed
Always terminates upon sale of either parcel
rationales: That describes an easement in gross.
Correct. It benefits a dominant parcel and runs with the land automatically.
It can be created by deed, among other methods.
It generally survives a sale of either parcel; it does not automatically terminate.

questions.stem: A utility company's easement to run power lines across a property is typically an example of:
options: Easement appurtenant
Easement in gross
Prescriptive easement only
Easement by necessity only
rationales: It does not benefit a specific dominant parcel.
Correct. It benefits a specific entity, characteristic of an easement in gross.
It is typically created by grant, not solely by prescription.
It is not created solely through necessity.

questions.stem: Merger as a method of easement termination occurs when:
options: The dominant tenement owner sells the property
The same person acquires both the dominant and servient tenements
The easement is used more frequently
A survey is recorded
rationales: A sale to a different owner does not itself terminate the easement.
Correct. Merger eliminates the two-separate-parcels requirement for an easement to exist.
Increased use does not terminate an easement.
Recording a survey does not itself terminate an easement.

questions.stem: Abandonment of an easement generally requires:
options: Mere non-use for any period
Conduct clearly showing intent to permanently stop using the easement
A written release only
Nothing; it is automatic after one year
rationales: Non-use alone is generally insufficient.
Correct. Clear conduct showing intent to permanently abandon is required.
A written release is a separate termination method, not required for abandonment specifically.
There is no automatic one-year abandonment rule described here.

questions.stem: An encroachment is best described as:
options: A recorded easement
An unauthorized physical intrusion of a structure onto neighboring land
A type of nuisance lawsuit
A boundary survey report
rationales: It is not itself a recorded easement.
Correct. It is an unauthorized physical intrusion onto neighboring property.
It is a physical condition, not itself a lawsuit type.
It is not the survey report itself, though a survey can reveal one.

questions.stem: A survey reveals a wall has sat fourteen inches onto a neighbor's lot for over twenty years without objection. A practical, commonly used resolution is:
options: Ignoring it since it has been that way for years
A negotiated, recorded boundary line agreement between the neighbors
Immediate forced demolition with no negotiation
Assuming the issue disappears at closing
rationales: Ignoring it leaves the issue unresolved and risks future disputes.
Correct. A recorded boundary line agreement is often the most practical, cost-effective resolution.
Forced demolition without negotiation is not the typical or most practical first step.
The issue does not disappear automatically at closing and must be disclosed.

questions.stem: Failing to object to a longstanding encroachment risks:
options: Nothing at all
The encroacher eventually establishing a prescriptive easement or similar claim
Automatic transfer of full ownership within one year
Immediate criminal liability for the property owner
rationales: Real legal risk can develop over time.
Correct. Undisturbed, continuous encroachment can support a prescriptive claim after the statutory period.
There is no automatic one-year full ownership transfer.
This is a civil property matter, not typically a criminal one.

questions.stem: Private nuisance differs from public nuisance because private nuisance:
options: Affects the broader community
Affects a particular person's use and enjoyment of their specific property
Can only be pursued by government agencies
Requires proof of a recorded easement
rationales: That describes public nuisance.
Correct. Private nuisance affects a specific owner's use and enjoyment.
Private nuisance is generally pursued by the affected private party.
Nuisance claims do not require a recorded easement.

options: Affects only one neighboring property
Affects the broader community and can be addressed by government or private parties
Is always resolved through a boundary survey
Cannot ever result in legal action
rationales: Public nuisance reaches beyond one property.
Correct. It affects the community broadly and multiple parties can pursue action.
A survey resolves boundary disputes, not nuisance claims generally.
Legal action is available for a genuine public nuisance.

questions.stem: A common defense to a nuisance claim is:
options: That the interference is not substantial under a reasonableness standard
That the defendant owns the property
That the plaintiff is a real estate licensee
That the county has issued a business license, which is always a complete defense
rationales: Correct. Courts apply a reasonableness standard; minor interference is not automatically actionable.
Property ownership alone is not a defense to causing a nuisance.
The plaintiff's occupation is irrelevant to the nuisance analysis.
A business license is a factor but not automatically a complete defense.

questions.stem: A licensed land surveyor's boundary survey primarily:
options: Insures title against defects
Establishes the precise legal location of property lines
Replaces the need for title insurance entirely
Determines zoning classification
rationales: Title insurance, not a survey, insures against title defects.
Correct. A survey establishes precise legal boundary locations.
A survey does not replace the separate function of title insurance.
Zoning classification is a separate governmental determination.

questions.stem: A preliminary title report differs from a boundary survey because the preliminary report:
options: Physically locates the boundary on the ground
Identifies recorded interests but does not resolve the physical boundary location
Is prepared by a licensed surveyor
Is unrelated to real estate transactions
rationales: Physical location on the ground is the survey's job, not the prelim's.
Correct. The prelim addresses recorded interests, not the physical boundary itself.
A prelim is prepared by a title company, not a surveyor.
It is directly related to real estate transactions.

questions.stem: A known boundary dispute or encroachment on a listed property should be:
options: Omitted if the neighbors have handled it informally for years
Disclosed as a material fact
Only disclosed if the buyer specifically asks
Left for the buyer's attorney to discover independently
rationales: Informal handling does not excuse disclosure of a known material fact.
Correct. A known boundary issue is a material fact requiring disclosure.
Disclosure duties do not depend on the buyer asking first.
The seller/agent has an affirmative disclosure duty, not a passive one.
